content: Sports Business News Life Real Estate Advertise Obituaries eNewspaper Legals CALIFORNIA COVID-19 infections growing across California, CDC says Mary Walrath-Holdridge Daniella Segura Palm Springs Desert Sun Sept. 2, 2026, 3:19 p.m. PT California is among 48 states across the nation where COVID-19 cases are growing, as summer draws to a close, according to the latest data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. The agency categorized COVID-19 activity as "very low" nationwide as of Aug. 28, though cases are consistently increasing. The uptick in COVID-19 is likely the result of what has come to be known as the "summer surge," a pattern that doctors have observed each year since around 2022. Unlike other respiratory illnesses such as the flu, COVID-19 tends to flare not only during the typical winter cold and flu season, but also toward the end of summer. The "summer surge" stems from multiple factors, including behavioral and environmental changes, such as spending more time indoors in air-conditioned spaces and returning to school, as well as the virus's life cycle and waning immunity, experts told USA TODAY in August. "COVID-19 is rising nationally, but from a low baseline," Dr. Syra Madad, infectious disease epidemiologist at Harvard’s Belfer Center and chief biopreparedness officer for New York City's public hospitals, told USA TODAY. "The increase became apparent in parts of the South and West during July and more clearly nationwide by late July and early August." Here's what to know as COVID-19 activity increases in the Golden State. COVID-19 in California, the rest of the nation As of Aug. 26, the CDC estimates that COVID-19 infections were growing or likely growing in 48 states, including California. The California Department of Public Health Respiratory Virus Dashboard shows that the test positivity rate is "moderate" across most of the state and "high" in Central California. The dashboard also shows COVID-19 hospital admission rates as "low." CDC wastewater data for the week ending Aug. 22 showed that California was among several states that had "moderate" levels of COVID-19 viral activity, while most other states were in the "low" or "very low" categories. Wastewater tracking involves testing community sewage for viruses and other germs, helping health officials monitor disease spread and identify trends before they appear in clinical testing data. COVID-19 prevention tips from CDC To prevent the spread of COVID-19, the CDC recommends the following strategies: Stay up to date with COVID-19 vaccines. By staying up to date with vaccination, the CDC says it does not prevent infection, but it does lower "the risk of getting very sick, being hospitalized, or dying from COVID-19." Practice good hygiene, including covering your coughs and sneezes, washing or sanitizing your hands often, and cleaning frequently touched surfaces. Take steps to improve indoor air quality. "This can mean bringing in fresh outside air, purifying indoor air, or gathering outdoors. Virus particles do not build up in the air outdoors as much as they do indoors," the CDC says. When you are sick, you should heed the following, the CDC says: Try to take precautions to prevent spread, including staying home and away from others (including people you live with who are not sick) if you have respiratory symptoms. Learn when you can go back to your normal activities. The CDC recommends that people with respiratory virus symptoms stay home until they are improving and fever-free for 24 hours, then take added precautions for five days to reduce the risk of spreading illness. If you have risk factors for severe illness, you should seek health care for testing and/or treatment. "Treatment may help lower your risk of severe illness, but it needs to be started within a few days of when your symptoms begin," the CDC says. Additional ways to protect yourself and others include wearing a mask and putting distance between yourself and others to limit the risk of spreading COVID-19, according to the CDC. By testing for COVID-19, it can help you decide on next steps, such as "getting treatment to reduce your risk of severe illness and taking steps to lower your chances of spreading COVID-19 to others," the agency says. content: breakingAmazon cargo plane overruns runway at Miami International Airport ABC News Live Video Local Shows Good Morning America ShopGMA Interest Successfully Added We'll notify you here with news about Turn on desktop notifications for breaking stories about interest? OffOn Stream on Updated COVID-19 vaccines are coming this fall. Will insurance cover them? Updated COVID-19 vaccines were approved by the FDA. ByAva Tsapatsaris September 2, 2026, 9:46 PM Share With cold and flu season approaching, public health specialists are warning that COVID-19 is still circulating. Updated COVID-19 vaccines were approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) on Thursday and are expected to become available across the U.S. this fall. But with changes to vaccine recommendations and eligibility, questions remain about how the shots will be covered. Related What you need to know about updated COVID vaccines following FDA approval What are insurers saying? Health insurance plans are expected to cover updated COVID-19 vaccines this season, according to AHIP, the trade association representing U.S. health insurance providers. In a statement to ABC News, AHIP confirmed that its members plan to cover the vaccines for the 2026-27 season, in line with a commitment the group made last year. In September 2025, AHIP said its member health plans would continue covering all vaccines recommended by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)'s Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) with no cost-sharing through the end of 2027. A sign in a pharmacy advertises the COVID-19 vaccine as the nation marks the fifth anniversary of the Covid-19 pandemic, March 11, 2025, in New York. Spencer Platt/Getty Images The Affordable Care Act requires insurers to cover vaccines recommended by ACIP, which votes on recommendations for how vaccines should be used after they are approved by the FDA, followed by sign-off from the CDC director. The committee has undergone significant changes since Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. removed all 17 of its previous members in June 2025 and replaced them with new appointees. Earlier this year, a federal judge stayed Kennedy's appointments to the panel. AHIP said coverage decisions are also based on each health plan's review of scientific and clinical evidence, as well as federal and state laws. What if you don't have insurance? People without health insurance may still be able to receive a COVID-19 vaccine for free. The HHS says uninsured adults may be able to find free COVID-19 vaccines through their state or local health departments. For children, the CDC’s Vaccines for Children program provides vaccines at no cost to eligible children, including those who are uninsured or Medicaid-eligible. The program automatically covers vaccines recommended by the ACIP and approved by the CDC. Related Severe COVID-19 linked to reactivation of some dormant viruses: Study What should you know before getting your COVID-19 vaccine? Moderna and Pfizer received FDA approval for their updated mRNA vaccines on Thursday. Sanofi also received approval for a protein-based shot. Popular Reads Grand Canyon trip turns tragic for 3 friends, as 2 confirmed dead after flash flood Sep 2 Unruly passenger arrested after being restrained with duct tape during flight 2 days ago Vietnam vets ask judge to block excavation work on Trump's 'triumphal arch' 2 days ago All the updated vaccines are approved for those aged 65 and older. Moderna's Spikevax is approved for people ages 6 months through 64 who have an underlying condition that puts them at high risk for severe COVID-19. Moderna's mNEXSPIKE is a newer mRNA vaccine that targets two specific parts of the spike protein, which the SARS-CoV-2 virus that causes COVID-19 uses to attach and infect human cells. It uses a lower dose of mRNA than Spikevax and is approved for people ages 12 through 64 who have an underlying condition that puts them at high risk for severe COVID-19. Pfizer's Comirnaty is approved for people ages 5 through 64 with at least one underlying condition that puts them at high risk for severe COVID-19. Sanofi's Nuvaxovid is approved for people ages 12 through 64 with at least one underlying condition that puts them at high risk for severe COVID-19. Related FDA withdraws publication of COVID, shingles vaccine research findings Underlying conditions that contribute to higher risk of severe COVID-19 include but are not limited to cancer, asthma, chronic lung disease, diabetes, heart conditions, mental health conditions and pregnancy. The American Academy of Family Physicians (AAFP) has issued its own recommendations amid changes to the federal vaccine recommendation process. AAFP recommends COVID-19 vaccination for all adults ages 19 and older. The group notes vaccination is especially important for people ages 65 and older, those at increased risk for severe COVID-19 and those who have never received a COVID-19 vaccine. The group also recommends COVID-19 vaccination for all children ages 6 months through 23 months and a risk-based approach for children and teens ages 2 through 18. COVID-19 vaccination is also recommended during any trimester of pregnancy and while breastfeeding. Other vaccines you may consider getting this season In addition to updated COVID-19 vaccines, public health specialists are recommending people stay up to date on influenza and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) vaccines. "Recommending and delivering all three seasonal vaccines early this fall remains our single most effective defense against preventable hospitalizations, critical illness, and death," said Dr. Ronald Nahas, president of the Infectious Diseases Society of America, during a briefing on Tuesday. A pharmacist prepares a shot of the Pfizer-BioNTech COVID-19 vaccine during an immunization event at the L.A. Care and Blue Shield of California Promise Health Plan Community Resource Center in the Panorama City neighborhood of Los Angeles, Oct. 24, 2025. Patrick T. Fallon/AFP via Getty Images The AAFP recommends an annual flu vaccine for everyone ages 6 months and older. Adults ages 65 and older should preferably receive a flu vaccine designed to produce a stronger immune response, such as a high-dose or adjuvanted vaccine, when available. For RSV, the CDC recommends a one-time vaccine for all adults ages 75 and older and adults ages 50 through 74 who are at increased risk for severe RSV illness. Infants who are not protected through maternal vaccination are recommended by the CDC to receive a long-acting RSV antibody, nirsevimab or clesrovimab. Children ages 8 through 19 months who are at increased risk for severe RSV disease and are entering their second RSV season are recommended to receive nirsevimab. Pregnant people are advised to receive Pfizer's RSV vaccine, Abrysvo, between 32 and 36 weeks of pregnancy during September through January by the CDC. The AAFP recommends extending this window through March. content: U.S. News World News Korea Regional Review Latin America Region Odd News Entertainment Movies Music TV Sports NFL MLB NBA Soccer Voices Photos News US News World News Entertainment Sports Archive Almanac U.S. News Sept. 2, 2026 / 2:33 PM Doctors release vaccine recommendations for RSV, influenza, COVID-19 By Lisa Hornung Medical groups have released vaccine recommendations this fall in lieu of guidance from the CDC. File Photo by Javier Aparico/EPA Sept. 2 (UPI) -- A group of medical organizations has released guidance on fall vaccinations against respiratory illnesses. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention usually launches a fall campaign to recommend seasonal vaccines for diseases like RSV, influenza and COVID-19. This year, however, the agency has not issued its updated recommendations for the respiratory virus season. In March, the American Academy of Pediatrics won a lawsuit against the federal government that blocked Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. from overhauling the childhood vaccine schedule. Kennedy and President Donald Trump have said that children get too many vaccines and have reduced the number of vaccines routinely recommended. They have also linked vaccines to autism, which has been proven untrue by research. In response, the American Academy of Pediatrics, the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists, the American Academy of Family Physicians, the Infectious Diseases Society of America each issued guidelines for fall immunizations. They based those guidelines on research from the American Medical Association and the University of Minnesota's Vaccine Integrity Project Last year, the CDC changed the COVID-19 recommendations to say that patients should talk to their own doctors. On Tuesday, the agency said, "the CDC states the recommendations for seasonal influenza vaccination from the July 2025 immunization schedule remain in effect for the 2026-2027 influenza season." It doesn't mention the new mRNA flu vaccine, approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration last month. "For more than 60 years, the United States has benefited from an established federal process for evaluating vaccine evidence and translating that science into recommendations for the American public. At the center of that process were the Centers for Disease Control and its Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices, the ACIP," CNN reported Dr. Bruce Gellin, board chair of the Vaccine Integrity Project and professor of medicine at Georgetown University, said at a press briefing. "Unfortunately today, the federal government is not fulfilling that responsibility in the way that it historically has. But the need for that work has not disappeared. Influenza, SARS-CoV-2 [COVID-19] and the RSV viruses will circulate again this fall and winter," Gellin said. "We cannot allow the breakdown of a federal process to create a vacuum in evidence-based vaccine guidance," he added. Dr. Sarah Nosal, president of the American Academy of Family Physicians, said in the news briefing that insurance companies have indicated they will cover the vaccines. "Vaccines are one of medicine's greatest success stories. They prevent serious illness, reduce hospitalizations and long-term complications and save lives," Nosal said in a press release. "As federal guidance evolves, the science behind vaccines remains strong. These recommendations are grounded in the latest evidence, informed by public health experts and shaped by what family physicians are seeing every day in their patients." content: About us Celebrating 125 Years Our history News and Stories Media Center Media Resources Contact Us Impact Our patients customers communities Our team members Our planet Impact library Shop Careers Press release Updated COVID-19 Vaccines Now Available at Walgreens Patients can schedule appointments in advance or walk in to receive their updated COVID-19, flu and other recommended vaccines at no cost with most insurance DEERFIELD, Ill., Sept. 4, 2026 – Walgreens is now offering 2026-2027 COVID-19 vaccines for eligible patients.1 With multiple viruses and seasonal illnesses expected to circulate this fall and winter, Walgreens is making it easy for patients to stay protected by offering COVID-19, flu, RSV, pneumococcal and other recommended vaccines during a single visit. Patients can walk into their local Walgreens pharmacy or schedule an appointment at Walgreens.com/ScheduleVaccine, through the Walgreens app, by texting “Flu” to 66879 or by calling 1-800-WALGREENS in most states. “As respiratory virus season ramps up, many people are thinking about how to protect themselves and their loved ones,” said Rick Gates, chief pharmacy officer, Walgreens. “Getting multiple recommended vaccines at the same time is a safe and effective way to reduce the risk of illness and help protect yourself, your family and your community heading into the fall and winter. Our goal is to make getting vaccinated as convenient as possible so patients can save time and stay protected.” Walgreens is continuing to invest in the vaccination experience this season through increased pharmacy staffing and expanded appointment availability, including the ability for patients to schedule appointments further in advance. As an added benefit, patients who get a vaccine at Walgreens can earn $15 in Walgreens Cash rewards on their next eligible in-store purchase of $5 or more as a myWalgreens® member. myWalgreens® member patients also receive 10% back in Walgreens Cash rewards on eligible purchases for the next 30 days.2 Frequently Asked Questions Why should I get the updated COVID-19 vaccine? The virus that causes COVID-19 evolves over time and immunity from prior vaccinations or infections naturally wanes. The updated 2026-2027 COVID-19 vaccine is specifically formulated to more closely match currently circulating variants. Receiving the updated COVID-19 vaccine helps you, your loved ones and your community stay protected as respiratory virus season approaches. When should I get the updated COVID-19 vaccine? For most people, the best time to get the updated COVID-19 vaccine is in the fall (September to October) before viruses begin spreading widely in your community. If you’re unsure when to get vaccinated, your Walgreens pharmacist can help you determine when you should receive the updated COVID-19 vaccine. Can I get the COVID-19 and flu vaccines at the same time? Yes, it is safe to receive multiple vaccines during the same appointment, including the COVID-19 and flu vaccines. Walgreens makes it easy to receive COVID-19, flu, RSV, pneumococcal and other recommended vaccinations during the same visit, helping individuals and families stay up to date on protection against multiple respiratory viruses while saving time. How much does getting the updated COVID-19 vaccine cost? The updated COVID-19 vaccine is available at no cost to you with most insurance. How can I get a COVID-19 vaccine at Walgreens? You can easily schedule an appointment for up to four people in a single visit by visiting Walgreens.com/ScheduleVaccine, through the Walgreens app, by texting “Flu” to 66879 or by calling 1-800-WALGREENS. Walk-ins are also welcome, and you can explore personalized vaccine recommendations through Walgreens’ digital scheduling tool. About Walgreens Founded in 1901, Walgreens (www.walgreens.com) proudly serves more than 9 million customers and patients each day across its nearly 8,000 stores throughout the U.S. and Puerto Rico. Walgreens has approximately 211,000 team members, including roughly 85,000 healthcare service providers, and is committed to being the first choice for pharmacy, retail and health services, building trusted relationships that create healthier futures for customers, patients, team members and communities. 1 Vaccines subject to availability. Walgreens administers applicable vaccinations for children ages three and older. State-, age-, and health-related restrictions may apply. 2 Must be a myWalgreens® member. Offer available for a limited time and valid for 14 days from vaccination date. Must scan coupon at checkout to earn rewards/activate. Coupon offer not valid in AR, NJ, or NY. Limit three coupons per person. See coupon for terms and restrictions. Vaccines subject to availability. Walgreens administers applicable vaccinations for children ages three and older. State-, age-, and health-related restrictions may apply. Additional terms and exclusions apply. Complete details, including Walgreens Cash rewards expiration dates, at Walgreens.com/offerdetails. $15 Offer Earn rewards on qualifying in-store purchases of $5+. Limit one storewide coupon redeemed per transaction, up to three redemptions per offer period. Maximum $45 Walgreens Cash rewards per member. 10% Offer Earn rewards on qualifying in-store purchases of $1+. Scan once to activate offer. Limit one offer per myWalgreens® member. Maximum $100 Walgreens Cash rewards. Offer valid for 30 days following activation. Media Contact Carly Kaplan media@walgreens.com Stay in the know Stay connected with the latest updates and the latest news from Walgreens delivered straight to your inbox. through the CVS Health app or CVS.com and walk-ins are accepted WOONSOCKET, R.I., Sept. 3, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- CVS Health® (NYSE: CVS) today announced that updated 2026-2027 COVID-19 vaccines are now available at CVS Pharmacy® and MinuteClinic® locations for patients at no-cost with most insurance plans. Appointments are available at CVS.com, MinuteClinic.com and through the CVS Health® app, and walk-ins are accepted at CVS Pharmacy and MinuteClinic. Continue Reading Updated COVID-19 vaccines available at CVS Pharmacy and MinuteClinic across the U.S. "We know patients value having convenient access to the vaccines and preventive care services they need," said Amy Compton-Phillips, MD, Executive Vice President and Chief Medical Officer, CVS Health. "With updated COVID-19 vaccines available at CVS Pharmacy and MinuteClinic, we're making it easier for people to get vaccinated close to home and on a schedule that works for them." CVS Pharmacy offers COVID-19 vaccinations for eligible patients based on state regulations*, while MinuteClinic provides vaccinations for patients beginning at 18 months of age. Pharmacists and MinuteClinic providers are available to answer questions and help patients make informed decisions about vaccination based on their individual health needs. Flexible scheduling for families and caregivers Vaccination appointments are available seven days a week, including evenings and weekends. Patients can schedule appointments at CVS Pharmacy and MinuteClinic for up to four people at the same time, helping families and caregivers get vaccinated together. If eligible, patients can also receive multiple recommended vaccinations during a single visit, including flu, RSV and other routine immunizations. The updated COVID-19 vaccine is available at no-cost through most insurance plans. For those who are uninsured, the cost at CVS Pharmacy and MinuteClinic varies depending on product type and eligibility. *CVS Pharmacy is actively monitoring vaccination requirements in Arizona, Louisiana and Oregon. Patients can check CVS.com, MinuteClinic.com or the CVS Health app for updated availability. About CVS Health CVS Health is a leading health solutions company simplifying health care one person, one family and one community at a time. As of June 30, 2026, the Company had approximately 9,000 retail pharmacy locations, more than 1,000 walk-in and primary care medical clinics and a leading pharmacy benefits manager with approximately 87 million plan members. The Company also serves an estimated 37 million people through a broad range of health insurance products and related services. The Company's integrated model uses personalized, technology driven services to connect people to simply better health, increasing access to quality care, delivering better outcomes, and lowering overall costs. title: Doctors say they’re filling a void left by CDC on vaccines. Here’s what to know about flu, Covid-19 and RSV this fall - CNN

excerpt_original: Doctors say they’re filling a void left by CDC on vaccines. Here’s what to know about flu, Covid-19 and RSV this fall CNN
priority_tier_reason: 可信机构来源或已成功抓获正文
content_title: Doctors say they’re filling a void left by CDC on vaccines. Here’s what to know about flu, Covid-19 and RSV this fall
content: Pharmacy manager Aylen Amestoy prepares to give a respiratory syncytial virus vaccine at a CVS Pharmacy in Miami in 2025. RSV, flu and Covid-19 vaccines are expected to be available at pharmacies and covered by insurance this fall and winter. Rebecca Blackwell/AP With children back in school and the looming threat of respiratory viruses like Covid-19, influenza and RSV on the horizon, many people may now be wondering how to stay healthy. Typically, the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention launches a fall campaign around this time of year, recommending seasonal immunizations such as the flu shot and Covid-19 vaccines. But under the second Trump administration, the agency has mostly been silent this year. The CDC hasn’t issued new recommendations for RSV immunization or Covid-19 vaccines for this season. Last year, the agency updated Covid-19 vaccine guidance to shift away from a broad recommendation, instead saying that patients must consult with a healthcare provider to get the vaccine. Ad Feedback On Tuesday, the agency updated its clinical guidance for the flu shot to follow last year’s recommendations, noting on its website that “the CDC states the recommendations for seasonal influenza vaccination from the July 2025 immunization schedule remain in effect for the 2026-2027 influenza season.” The update does not mention the first mRNA flu vaccine, which was approved by the US Food and Drug Administration last month for use in older adults. To help fill the void, the American Medical Association and the University of Minnesota’s Vaccine Integrity Project launched their own independent reviews of this fall’s vaccines – including those for flu , Covid and RSV – which was published Wednesday in the medical journal JAMA. The review papers helped inform 2026-27 respiratory virus immunization recommendations released Wednesday by several medical groups, including the American Academy of Pediatrics, American Academy of Family Physicians, American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists and the Infectious Diseases Society of America. “For more than 60 years, the United States has benefited from an established federal process for evaluating vaccine evidence and translating that science into recommendations for the American public. At the center of that process were the Centers for Disease Control and its Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices, the ACIP,” Dr. Bruce Gellin, board chair of the Vaccine Integrity Project and professor of medicine at Georgetown University, said at a news briefing. “Unfortunately today, the federal government is not fulfilling that responsibility in the way that it historically has. But the need for that work has not disappeared. Influenza, SARS-CoV-2 and the RSV viruses will circulate again this fall and winter,” Gellin said. “Clinicians will still have patients to care for. Parents will still have decisions to make for their children, and older Americans, pregnant women and people with underlying health conditions will still need to know how best to protect themselves,” he said. “We cannot allow the breakdown of a federal process to create a vacuum in evidence-based vaccine guidance.” The US Department of Health and Human Services has not responded to CNN’s request for comment on the groups’ recommendations. The recommendations provide guidance on which fall vaccines are recommended for whom and when is the optimal time to get them. Flu and RSV immunizations are now available at major pharmacies, and updated Covid-19 shots were recently approved by the FDA and are becoming available. “And really reassuringly, insurers have indicated to the major groups that they will cover these respiratory virus immunizations,” Dr. Sarah Nosal, president of the American Academy of Family Physicians, said in the news briefing. “Vaccines are one of medicine’s greatest success stories. They prevent serious illness, reduce hospitalizations and long-term complications and save lives,” Nosal said in a news release. “As federal guidance evolves, the science behind vaccines remains strong. These recommendations are grounded in the latest evidence, informed by public health experts and shaped by what family physicians are seeing every day in their patients.” RSV immunization Who should get it The groups eligible for RSV immunizations include older adults, pregnant people and infants. “People age 50 and older with high-risk conditions, and everyone over 75 years old, should get one dose,” Nosal said. “This is not an annual vaccine. If you got one before, you do not need a new one this year. Getting one should protect you throughout the entire season.” During pregnancy, RSV vaccination is recommended in the third trimester, between weeks 32 and 36. Children younger than 8 months should be immunized against RSV using a monoclonal antibody unless their mother got an RSV vaccination during pregnancy, said Dr. Andrew Racine, president of the American Academy of Pediatrics. “If the mother’s immunization status is unknown, that child should be immunized,” Racine said in the briefing. He added that children between 8 months and 19 months of age who are in certain high-risk groups for severe disease are also recommended to get the RSV monoclonal antibody. And a single dose of RSV vaccine is recommended for adults who have weakened immune systems. “Immunosuppressed individuals are at higher risk for severe disease than immunocompetent individuals,” Dr. Dan Barouch, director of the Center for Virology and Vaccine Research at Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, who was not involved in the new recommendations, said in an email. “The vaccines are also generally less effective in immunosuppressed individuals compared with immunocompetent individuals.” When to get it For older adults, RSV vaccinations are typically recommended in late summer and early fall. The advice slightly changed this year for pregnant people. “ACOG now recommends that pregnant individuals receive a single dose of the maternal RSV vaccine, Abrysvo, from September 1 through March 1 instead of only through January 31,” Dr. Christina Davidson, chief medical officer of the American College of Obstetricians & Gynecologists, said in the news briefing. “We made this change because the RSV disease season is now occurring later in the spring, and it is also more severe than it used to be,” Davidson said. “The extension of the eligibility window will help provide pregnant patients and their infants with additional protection.” For infants, the RSV monoclonal antibody is typically recommended around virus season, from October through March. Seasonal flu shots Who should get it Everyone 6 months and older is recommended to get an annual flu shot. “On average, flu vaccines reduce the risk of needing to go to the doctor by 30% to 60%,” Nosal said. “Adults 65 years and older should get an enhanced flu vaccine, one that is high-dose, adjuvanted or recombinant, when it’s available,” she said. “But do not delay your vaccination if that one’s not available.” And for the first time, an mRNA-based flu vaccine is available for use in adults 50 and older. The flu vaccine is also recommended during pregnancy, but pregnant people should avoid the nasal spray version, according to the recommendations. “Pregnant and postpartum people still have a significantly higher risk of developing serious complications from infection compared with non-pregnant people,” Davidson said. “The inactivated or recombinant influenza vaccines remain the only vaccines that are recommended for use in pregnancy in any trimester, so please work with your OB care clinician or pharmacist to get these,” she said. “Most importantly, if you are able to get the vaccine while you are pregnant, the immunity will also, in part, pass on to your baby.” When to get it October is the ideal time to get vaccinated, Nolan said, because “protection wanes throughout the season.” Some providers use the slogan “ flu before boo ” to remind people to get a flu shot before Halloween. Updated Covid-19 vaccines Who should get it Getting an updated Covid-19 vaccine is recommended for adults. “If you’re older than 19, we recommend getting the Covid-19 vaccine,” Nosal said. “This is especially important for people who are 65 years and older, at increased risk for severe Covid infection and those who’ve never received a Covid-19 vaccine,” she said. “For those adults 65 years and older, they should receive a second dose of the updated Covid-19 vaccine six months after that season’s initial dose to help maintain protection as immunity wanes over time.” The vaccine is also recommended for infants between 6 months and 23 months of age, and children in certain high-risk groups or those whose families request vaccination. And for people who are immunocompromised, the annual updated Covid-19 vaccine is recommended for ages 6 months and older. Last year, the CDC recommended Covid-19 vaccines based on conversations with the patient’s healthcare provider, known as shared decision-making, Barouch noted, but the agency “also emphasized that the risk-benefit of the vaccines is most favorable for individuals who are at higher risk of severe disease.” Davidson, of ACOG, said the vaccine is also recommended during pregnancy. “The most important message is this: If you are pregnant, considering pregnancy or are a new or breastfeeding parent, please get your vaccine or your annual booster. All four of the available Covid vaccines are safe for you,” Davidson said. Moderna offers two mRNA shots, Pfizer and BioNTech have another, and Sanofi and Novavax offer a more traditional protein-based version. “A recommendation for the Covid vaccine is based on more than five years of research and millions of administered doses,” Davidson said. “I want to emphasize that the evidence has found no increased risk of miscarriage, stillbirth, preterm birth, small for gestational age birth or birth defects. The risks of complications from Covid for pregnant people and their babies, however, is high. So please get the vaccine.” When to get it It’s recommended to get the updated vaccine now, but if you have been recently infected with Covid, experts advise waiting four to six months before getting the vaccine. The updated Covid-19 vaccine “targets the most recent strain that’s been circulating, and so if you want to update your protection, that’s the best way to do it,” Dr. Sandra Adamson Fryhofer, president-elect of the American Medical Association, said in the news briefing. “You know, your computer constantly needs to be updated. Well, your immune system, your immunity needs to be constantly updated too,” she said. “You’re going to get your most protection in those first few months after the vaccine. So if you have a big event – if you have to go to a wedding, or if you’re going on some fabulous trip, or you’re going to a fabulous birthday party, or just any birthday party or get-together – think about getting that vaccine a couple of weeks before that event, so you’ll stay healthy and well.” See all topics

COVID-19 cases are ticking up in almost every U.S. state as summer draws to a close, according to the latest data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. COVID-19 activity was still categorized overall as "very low" nationwide by the agency as of Aug. 28, though cases are consistently increasing. This is likely the result of what has come to be known as the "summer surge," a pattern that doctors have observed each year since around 2022. Unlike other respiratory illnesses such as the flu, COVID-19 tends to flare not only during the typical winter cold and flu season, but also toward the end of summer. Experts previously told USA TODAY that this is likely caused by multiple factors, including behavioral and environmental changes (the amount of time spent cooped up in AC, going back to school, etc.), as well as the virus's life cycle and how our immunity to it waxes and wanes. "COVID-19 is rising nationally but from a low baseline," Dr. Syra Madad, infectious disease epidemiologist at Harvard’s Belfer Center and chief biopreparedness officer for New York City's public hospitals, previously told USA TODAY. "The increase became apparent in parts of the South and West during July and more clearly nationwide by late July and early August." The latest CDC data shows that at least one state has already entered the "high activity" category for the virus. Here's what to know, including state-by-state updates: Where COVID-19 cases are growing: See map As of Aug. 26, the CDC estimates that COVID-19 infections were growing or likely growing in 48 states. Only one state, Iowa, did not provide data. Rhode Island and Washington, DC, were the only locations where viral activity remained the same week over week. Where activity is high: See map According to the most recent CDC wastewater data for the week ending Aug. 22, COVID-19 viral activity was consistently highest in the southern United States. Only one state, Texas, had "very high" levels, while Mississippi reported "high" activity. A handful of states across regions, including California, Nevada, Florida, Rhode Island, Louisiana and Washington, had "moderate" levels, while most other states were in the "low" or "very low" categories. Wastewater tracking is the testing of community sewage for viruses and other germs to help health officials monitor disease spread and trends, often before cases show up in clinical testing data. With Cases Rising in Nearly Every State, Watch for These Symptoms As summer winds down, COVID-19 activity is increasing nationwide. Here’s where cases are the highest and how to protect yourself. Updated Sept. 4, 2026, 6:13 PM UTC / Source: TODAY Caroline Kee Health reporter Skip to table of contents 0 of 4 minutes, 47 secondsVolume 0% Press shift question mark to access a list of keyboard shortcuts Keyboard ShortcutsEnabledDisabled Play/PauseSPACE Increase Volume↑ Decrease Volume↓ Seek Forward→ Seek Backward← Captions On/Offc Fullscreen/Exit Fullscreenf Mute/Unmutem Decrease Caption Size- Increase Caption Size+ or = Seek %0-9 Settings OffCCEnglish Font Color White Font Opacity 100% Font Size 100% Font Family Arial Character Edge None Background Color Black Background Opacity 50% Window Color Black Window Opacity 0% Reset WhiteBlackRedGreenBlueYellowMagentaCyan 100%75%50%25% 200%175%150%125%100%75%50% ArialCourierGeorgiaImpactLucida ConsoleTahomaTimes New RomanTrebuchet MSVerdana NoneRaisedDepressedUniformDrop Shadow WhiteBlackRedGreenBlueYellowMagentaCyan 100%75%50%25%0% WhiteBlackRedGreenBlueYellowMagentaCyan 100%75%50%25%0% Auto540p (1921 kbps)1080p (5110 kbps)720p (3680 kbps)540p (1921 kbps)360p (1041 kbps)270p (601 kbps)270p (381 kbps) Live 00:01 04:45 04:47 Add to Google Trump Signs Executive Order on Childhood Vaccine Schedule 04:47 Share Add to Google Savewith a NBCUniversal Profile Although foodborne pathogens have been in the spotlight all summer, another highly contagious virus is now surging in the United States: coronavirus. After a long lull, COVID-19 cases are on the rise in nearly part of the country. So if you’ve been plagued by coughing and sniffles recently, it may be time to take a COVID test. As of Sept. 2, the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention estimates that COVID infections are growing or likely growing in 47 states and declining in zero states. COVID-19 activity is still considered low, nationally, the CDC says. However, rates are increasing quickly in many states, especially in the South and West. Texas is currently reporting the highest levels of COVID in wastewater of any state, per CDC data. One school district in south Texas was forced to close for several days due to the rapid spread of COVID. San Perlita ISD shut down from Aug. 25-26 to “protect the health and safety” of students and staff, the district said in a notice. The current wave is not unexpected, according to experts. The SARS-CoV-2 virus can spread year-round, but it has settled into a distinctive seasonal pattern in the U.S. since the pandemic began. “We’ve had two waves (every year). One in the middle to late summer, and the other during the winter,” Dr. William Schaffner, an infectious disease specialist and professor of medicine at Vanderbilt University Medical Center, tells TODAY.com. While the country was focused on a massive outbreak of cyclospora last month, COVID was creeping up too, data show. Although the respiratory virus may not be top of mind for many Americans, says Schaffner, it’s certainly spreading — just in time for back-to-school season. Is the U.S. facing a new COVID surge and when will cases peak? Here’s what we know about the latest trends and how to stay safe. 2026 Summer COVID-19 Surge The U.S. is experiencing a late summer COVID-19 wave, experts say. “The national data is beginning to tick up, but it’s not a substantial increase yet,” says Schaffner. According to the latest CDC analysis, the overall level of COVID activity in wastewater was still “very low” nationally during the week ending Aug. 29. However, CDC data show 13 states are reporting moderate, high or very high levels of COVID activity: Alabama Alaska Arizona California Florida Georgia Hawaii Louisiana Mississippi Montana Nevada Texas Washington The latest data from WastewaterSCAN, a Stanford University-run infectious disease monitoring program, show that the level of SARS-CoV-2 activity in wastewater is “high” nationwide, with a significant upward trend in the last 21 days. “We’ve been seeing a pretty steady increase since late June across the (U.S.),” Amanda Bidwell, WastewaterSCAN Scientific Program Manager, tells TODAY.com. By late August, SARS-CoV-2 concentrations had jumped up 140% compared to July 2026. “In the West and South we’ve surpassed the peak concentrations observed during the winter peak (2025-2026),” Bidwell added. Map of COVID-19 Wastewater Viral Activity Levels by State, Aug. 22-29CDC At least 29 states and territories in the U.S. are experiencing active COVID outbreaks, according to an Aug. 31 report from Pandemic Mitigation Collaborative’s data tracker. “That is troubling, especially if you’re in one of those areas,” Michael Hoerger, Ph.D., assistant professor at Tulane University School of Medicine who leads the PMC. Recommended Deals DealsLululemon Leggings, Hoodies and More for Fall — Up to 50% Off Deals DealsWhen Is Amazon’s Fall Prime Day? Here’s What We Know So Far However, the experts emphasize that the current wave appears to be less severe than what we’ve seen in previous years. In 2025, the U.S. experienced an intense summer surge fueled by the “Stratus” variant, which lasted into the fall. “We are still seeing lower SARS-CoV-2 concentrations compared to this time last year,” says Bidwell. During the week ending Aug. 29, about 6% of COVID-19 tests came back positive — this same time last year, the weekly test positivity rate was over 11%, per CDC data. It’s unclear how severe this late summer wave could become or when it may peak. “We’re expecting transmission to peak about a week into September,” says Hoerger, adding that the regional spread could shift as well. Only time will tell, the experts note. As temperatures drop and millions of children return to school, this could create more opportunities for the virus to spread. “We need to be very cautious,” says Schaffner. Which COVID-19 Variants Are Spreading? The current COVID wave is being driven by a mixture of familiar variants, says Bidwell. The latest WastewaterSCAN data is detecting XFG, LF.7, NB.1.8.1, and BA.3.2. XFG.1.1 and its sublineages accounted for nearly half of all cases in the U.S. in July, according to the latest data from the CDC. XFG, aka Stratus, is a highly contagious recombinant strain which overtook the Nimbus (NB.1.8.1) variant last summer, Dr. Albert Ko, professor of public health, epidemiology and medicine at Yale School of Public Health, tells TODAY.com. “It’s still within the family of past omicron variants (from) this past year, so it’s not a big jump in terms of being different. That’s probably why we’re not seeing a big peak this summer,” Ko adds. Less than 10% of cases are being fueled by the BA.3.2 variant, aka Cicada, per CDC data. The heavily mutated strain emerged earlier this year and began spreading rapidly worldwide. However, Cicada hasn’t seemed to take off in the U.S., the experts note. While there hasn’t been a major shift or mutation in the latest variants, the virus may still evolve in the future, Hoerger notes. “The fact that we are not seeing an entirely new variant doesn’t mean COVID is not going to cause severe disease,” Ko says. COVID Symptoms 2026 The symptoms of the COVID-19 variants fueling the summer wave are similar to those caused by other omicron strains. These usually appear within two to 14 days of exposure to the virus. Common signs of COVID-19 in 2026, per the CDC, include: Cough Sore throat Congestion Fatigue Fever Chills Shortness of breath Headache Nausea and vomiting Diarrhea The symptoms of COVID and other common respiratory viruses are very similar, which is why testing is important. If you test negative using a rapid at-home antigen test, the CDC recommends taking another test after 48 hours to be confident that you aren’t infected. Most people recover from COVID-19 on their own, but some groups are at higher risk of severe illness or hospitalization, says Schaffner. These include adults over the age of 65, infants, individuals with weak immune systems or underlying conditions, and people who have never gotten a COVID vaccine. The infection can be treated with antivirals, which reduce symptom severity and duration when taken early. COVID Quarantine Guidelines for 2026 If you get sick with COVID-19, the CDC recommends staying home and isolating from others who aren’t sick until you feel better. You can go back to your normal activities once your symptoms have improved and you’ve been fever-free without medication for at least 24 hours, the CDC says. While recovering, the experts recommend practicing social distancing, especially from immunocompromised people, and wearing a well-fitted N95 respirator or KN95. If you don’t have COVID-19, you can take actions to protect yourself, says Schaffner. These include wearing a mask in crowded indoor settings, avoiding contact with sick people and staying up to date on vaccines. Is the New COVID-19 Booster Available? For the last few years, the COVID-19 vaccine has been reformulated every summer to provide protection against the latest strains circulating. In May, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration voted to recommend the updated COVID vaccine for 2026-2027 target the XFG variant, NBC News reported previously. On Aug. 28, the FDA approved the monovalent 2026-2027 COVID vaccines from Moderna, Pfizer-BioNTech, and Novavax-Sanofi, the Associated Press reported. “The new shots will cover what’s anticipated to be circulating this fall and winter,” says Schaffner. The new COVID shots are expected to be rolled out at pharmacies, clinics and hospitals in September, experts say. “It could be later if there’s any kind of snag,” says Hoerger. “That’s frustrating because we’ve got outbreaks happening now,” he adds. The CDC has not yet issued recommendations around the 2026-2027 COVID vaccines. Last year, the agency shifted its COVID-19 vaccine guidelines from a universal recommendation to a shared clinical-decision making model for everyone ages 6 months and older. “This means you should talk with your healthcare provider, whether it’s a doctor or nurse, or a pharmacist first,” says Ko. The COVID vaccine protects people from severe illness, hospitalization and death, per the CDC. It can also lower the risk of developing long COVID, Hoerger adds. That’s why most medical experts recommend that everyone who is eligible get a new COVID booster this fall. It’s especially important for high-risk groups and pregnant women to get vaccinated, Schaffner adds. “At this point, many of us have been exposed multiple times to COVID, so we are building up immunity. But there is a benefit to getting vaccines, especially before the winter,” says Ko. content: Log in Log in Forgot Password Close News News Comment Features Obituaries Business Sport Magazine Review Saturday Money Travel Galleries Weather Puzzles Lead story Share Fourth jabs won’t be necessary, say experts JCVI says current boosters are protecting vulnerable as evidence grows of omicron being milder Laura Donnelly Sarah Knapton Simon Johnson FOURTH jabs are not currently needed, the Government’s scientific advisers have said, as evidence grows that omicron is far milder than previous variants. The Joint Committee on Vaccination and Immunisation (JCVI) announced last night that boosters continued to provide high levels of protection against severe disease from omicron in older adults, including the most vulnerable. 40pc The proportion of people with Covid in Scotland’s hospitals who are being primarily treated for other conditions Its analysis found that three months after receiving a third jab, protection against hospitalisation among over-65s remained at about 90 per cent. Ministers have been exploring the possibility of a fourth jab for several weeks, after Israel, considered a global pioneer in Covid vaccinations, launched such a programme last month. But Prof Wei Shen Lim, the JCVI’s chairman of Covid-19 immunisation, said: “The current data show the booster dose is continuing to provide high levels of protection against severe disease, even for the most vulnerable older age groups. For this reason, the committee has concluded there is no immediate need to introduce a second booster dose, though this will continue to be reviewed.” It came as Covid numbers in Britain fell for a third day in a row and evidence emerged that hospitalisations arising from Covid cases were 12 times lower than during last year’s winter peak. There were 178,250 cases reported in the UK yesterday, down from 179,756 the previous day and a fall of more than 11,000 from the same day last week. Figures from Scotland show that just 1 per cent of people who test positive for Covid are ending up in hospital, down from 12 per cent last January. Meanwhile, figures from England show the number of patients in mechanical ventilation beds has fallen to 728, a decline of 63 in a week and the lowest number since October. During a visit to King’s College Hospital in south London, Sajid Javid, the Health Secretary, said: “When we look at omicron versus the previous variants, of course there are some encouraging signs; we know now that omicron is less severe.” However, Mr Javid emphasised the need for people to come forward for their booster jab, with the NHS facing “challenging times”. On the same visit, Amanda Pritchard, the head of the NHS, said a fortnight of further hospital admissions for Covid-19 was “already baked in”, as some NHS staff faced “the steepest climb of the pandemic yet”. Staff absences because of Covid isolation are continuing to cause severe pressures on services, with warnings that this could continue for some weeks. The JCVI said that rolling out a fourth jab programme “would add to the significant existing operational pressures” for the vaccine rollout and the rest of the NHS, noting that “the current omicron wave is progressing very swiftly, offering limited time for additional vaccine programme measures to have a substantial impact within this wave”. They said that even in the most vulnerable, a fourth jab would provide “limited additional benefit against severe disease at this present time” and that the main aim of the vaccination programme remained prevention of severe disease, not protection against mild or asymptomatic infection. Protecting against all infection would require regular jabs, as often as every three months, which “is not considered a sustainable long-term strategy” the JCVI said. They added that alternative vaccines, including variant-specific jabs, which may become available later this year, may prove better suited to providing long-term protection against novel variants. The comments echo the remarks made earlier this week by Sir Andrew Pollard, the chairman of the JCVI, who told The Daily Telegraph that “more strong evidence is needed” before the rollout of a fourth vaccine. He said: “We can’t vaccinate the planet every four to six months. It’s not sustainable or affordable. In the future, we need to target the vulnerable.” It came amid increasing evidence that omicron is milder than previous variants. Latest figures show an increase in hospitalisations, with 2,434 admissions yesterday, up from 2,080. But NHS data show that in some areas as many as 45 per cent of patients in hospital with Covid were admitted for other reasons. There were 13,045 people included in the official Covid hospital figures by Jan 4, but 4,825 of them had been admitted for other reasons. This means 37 per cent of Covid hospital patients were admitted for other reasons – compared with a figure of 24 per cent earlier this month. The figures show that, in the week ending Jan 4, hospital cases of “incidental Covid” rose by 135 per cent, from 2,065 to 4,845. The number of patients classed as “primarily Covid” saw lower growth, of 83 per cent, from 4,479 to 8,200. The Midlands had the highest proportion of incidental cases, at 45 per cent. In London, the percentage of non-Covid cases included in the figures hit a high of 44.7 per cent on Jan 2 but has since fallen to 38.2 per cent. The latest statistics also show that deaths from Covid in care homes are up to 10 times lower than this time last year even though there have been a greater number of outbreaks. Calculations by The Telegraph also suggest that in England just 2 per cent of cases are ending up in hospital compared with 12 per cent last winter. New data from Public Health Scotland also show that only one in 100 people who recently tested positive for Covid required hospital care, compared with one in eight at the end of January. The Public Health Scotland study found that four in 10 people in Scotland’s hospitals with Covid were being primarily treated for other conditions, rather than being admitted because they required care for the virus, piling pressure on Nicola Sturgeon to scrap her hardline restrictions. Editorial Comment: Britain needs a route back to normality Share Enlarge Coronavirus Share Infected Scots in hospital for other reasons, data show Simon JohnsonScottish Political Editor FOUR in 10 people with Covid in Scotland’s hospitals were primarily admitted for other reasons, according to an official analysis published yesterday. Only 60 per cent of acute hospital admissions involving patients with Covid were determined to be “because of” the virus, a study by Public Health Scotland (PHS) found. This figure was a sharp reduction on the 68 per cent recorded in a previous PHS study covering March to August last year, when the delta variant was the dominant strain. PHS said that it was important to differentiate between patients who were admitted to hospital “because” they required treatment for Covid with those whose admission was “coincident” with testing positive. The agency said this was because “knowing this information can help signal whether population-level changes in public health measures may be warranted, such as a tightening or easing of restrictions”. In another extraordinary finding that raised questions about Nicola Sturgeon’s restrictions, the study said only one in 100 Scots who catch Covid require hospital care after the UK’s vaccination programme and the spread of the milder omicron variant. It found the proportion of people who needed hospital care after getting the virus dropped from 12 per cent in January last year to just 1 per cent in December. When age was taken into account, the report said people were 12.5 more times to be hospitalised with Covid if they are unvaccinated than if they had received a booster or third vaccine dose. Nearly two thirds of confirmed, probable or possible omicron cases (64 per cent) recorded since the start of November were found to have been contracted by the under-40s, who have lower vaccination levels. Despite this, the study said there had been a 31 per cent increase in hospital admissions in Scotland in the week ending Dec 28, with the highest number involving patients aged over 80. The findings were based on an analysis of patient records at NHS Greater Glasgow and Clyde and NHS Grampian at the end of December and beginning of January, with both health boards recording “reasonably similar” results. They further increase the pressure on the First Minister over her hardline restrictions in Scotland after she admitted on Wednesday she was rethinking her strategy for tackling Covid thanks to omicron’s increased transmissibility. In a major about-turn that brings her approach more in line with that of Boris Johnson, she disclosed her government will shortly unveil a blueprint for Scotland to live with the virus in the long term that would be “more proportionate and sustainable and less restrictive”. She admitted that using restrictions to tackle the variant were less effective after figures showed the proportion of Scots with the virus doubled from one in 40 to one in 20 over the festive period. This was similar to many areas of England, where no new measures on social distancing, licensed premises and large events were introduced. The UK Government’s Covid dashboard yesterday showed that with 2,079 cases per 100,000 Scotland had a higher rate than England on 1,787. Dr Sandesh Gulhane, a GP and the Scottish Tories’ shadow health secretary, said the PHS report had provided “a crucial missing piece of the puzzle through this pandemic” by disclosing four out of 10 Covid patients were not being treated primarily for the virus. He said: “This is a significant percentage, which could mean the difference between whether restrictions are lifted or increased when it comes to decision time for the Government.” Noting the report covered only two of the largest health board areas, he added: “The SNP must commit to providing the full data, as soon as possible, so that we can make sure our Covid response remains balanced and proportionate in the months ahead.” But Humza Yousaf, the SNP’s Health Secretary, said: “This analysis suggests that Covid-19 continues to increase the pressure on the NHS in Scotland – with the majority of Covid-19 patients admitted to hospital because of the infection and admissions continuing to affect a disproportionately greater number of older people.” Prof Jason Leitch, Scotland’s national clinical director, said patients with Covid imposed an additional burden on the NHS whether they required treatment for the virus or another condition. He said: “A failing transplant is much harder to manage if a patient has a positive Covid test for example.” Prof Linda Bauld, a public health expert who advises the Scottish Government, noted that daily case numbers will become less relevant as positive lateral flow tests no longer need a PCR confirmation. However, the PHS research also disclosed that Scotland’s troubled Test and Protect contacting tracing system was failing to complete a growing proportion of cases. This means attempts to reach the person who had tested positive had failed or they did not provide details of their contacts. Incomplete attempts made up 12.4 per cent of cases in the week ending Dec 5, nearly trebling to 35.8 per cent in the week ending Dec 26. Even among the completed cases, more than a quarter took longer than three days. Commentary Share Time for Scotland’s opposition to force the end of ‘lockdown by stealth’ Alan Cochrane This was the week that Nicola Sturgeon appeared to accept that there was more than one way to stop a pandemic surging out of control and that a programme of heavier restrictions wasn’t among them. However, if we’re to believe that this was a genuine Damascene conversion to something much more in tune with Boris Johnson’s approach in England, then the Scottish First Minister must surely abandon her insistence that she plans to keep her controls in place for another 10 days. And it is now up to what opposition there is at Holyrood to force the end of what others have called a “lockdown by stealth”. Her terminology this week suggested a change of emphasis, with my colleague, Simon Johnson, reporting that she told the Scottish Parliament she was planning a blueprint to live with the virus in the long term that would be “more proportionate and sustainable and less restrictive”. It was essentially an admission that hard-line restrictions weren’t effective anymore. Sadly, however, none of the above meant that the restrictions she’d imposed to take effect from Boxing Day, with nightclubs closed, table service only in pubs and severe limits on all gatherings, whether inside or out, would be scrapped. They’re still supposed to last until Jan 17. Unless, of course, she has another change of heart. After all, she initially said that she wouldn’t change the self-isolation rule from 10 days to seven, which the Prime Minister did for England on Dec 22 when everyone in Scotland – from the hospitality industry to public services, all stretched by staff shortages, were pleading with her to follow suit. In an incredible explanation, she insisted that she had to adhere to advice from her government’s advisers, while Mr Johnson listened to his experts – plainly ignoring the fact that many in both groups were the same people. Then – and for no other reason than fear of being seen to be “copying Boris” – she refused to budge even to the extent of telling Holyrood on Dec 29 that she’d think about it “in a few days”. And so, this week, she did what she should have done two weeks ago and reduced the quarantine period to seven days. Also in the past week – but a day after it had been announced in London – her government abandoned the requirement for airport passenger checks, with Humza Yosaf, her hapless health minister, complaining about England’s “unilateral” behaviour on the issue. Ms Sturgeon has her first opportunity to revisit things in four days’ time when she delivers her Covid update to Holyrood. The huge increase in cases caused by the omicron variant is still causing major problems in Scotland – Army personnel have been called in to assist medical teams in Grampian and an additional 500 special police officers and trainees are being drafted in to fill vacancies in forces all over the country. But there are clear signs that while it is more transmissible, omicron is causing much less serious illness and leads to fewer hospital admissions. Figures released yesterday revealed that only one in a hundred people who catch Covid require hospital care following the UK’s vaccination programme, with Public Health Scotland reporting that the proportion of people who need hospital care after getting the virus dropped from 12 per cent in January last year to 1 per cent in December. The study also found that four in 10 people in hospital with Covid were being treated for other conditions, rather than requiring medical care for the virus. An urgent rethink of Scotland’s remaining Covid restrictions is necessary and it is up to opposition politicians to force a change in the coming days. Coronavirus Share Strict Welsh curbs fail to stem surge in cases Drakeford calls England ‘global outlier’ despite infections in Principality rising three times faster India McTaggart Alex Clark COVID case rates in Wales are rising almost three times faster than those in England despite tougher restrictions, the latest figures show. People in Wales have been living under alert-level-two measures – including mandatory face coverings indoors, a six-person limit for meeting in public places and the closure of nightclubs – since Boxing Day. Despite the measures, the country’s Covid cases have almost doubled since Dec 26, with an increase of 94 per cent, according to government data. England’s cases have increased by 34 per cent. Under England’s Plan B measures – less strict than in Wales – people have been told to work from home where possible, wear face coverings on public transport and in public places and show proof of Covid vaccination status to access large events and nightclubs. Prof Robert Dingwall, a former government Covid adviser, from Nottingham Trent University, said the omicron variant in Wales was “driving an increase which is not really being contained by these extra restrictions”. He said: “All of the extra interventions put in place by the Welsh Government really do not seem to have had any impact.” He added that the same scenario is taking place in certain places in France “which have a lot more restrictions, but are also having big waves of Covid, especially in the major cities”. “Omicron is so infectious that actually nothing you do makes much difference,” he said. It came as Mark Drakeford, the Welsh First Minister, confirmed yesterday that alert-level-two measures would remain for at least one more week, with case rates “rising steeply”. “Cases are far higher now than they were at the peak of all previous waves,” Mr Drakeford said as he warned that the “peak” of the wave could be another 10 to 14 days away. “Omicron is now the dominant form of the virus in Wales and cases are rising rapidly,” he said, adding that previous Covid waves “are nothing compared to the size and speed” of the variant. At a press conference Mr Drakeford said England was a “global outlier” in its response to omicron and accused the Government of being “politically paralysed”. He said the Prime Minister “is unable to secure an agreement through his Cabinet to take the actions that his advisers have been telling him ought to have been taken”. Official figures show there are more than 2,300 cases per 100,000 people across Wales, compared with 1,271 across England.
